🤖 THREEHALVES — THE CENTAUR ROBOT Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall teleoperated robot developed by Satyress. Its design combines a human-like torso and arms with a powerful four-legged chassis, creating a mechanical centaur built for environments that are too dangerous for humans. The idea behind Threehalves is simple: instead of sending a person into extreme heat, unstable terrain, darkness, hazardous industrial environments or disaster zones, a skilled operator can control the robot remotely and perform the work from a safer location. Unlike many humanoid robots, Threehalves is designed around tools and equipment that humans already use. Its modular limbs and quick-connect system allow it to be adapted for different tasks, while its four-legged platform provides stability on difficult terrain. The most unsettling part is probably its appearance. With its enormous size, humanoid body, four mechanical legs and distinctive horned head, Threehalves looks less like a traditional industrial machine and more like something from a science-fiction horror movie. But behind the terrifying design is a serious engineering concept: putting the machine in danger instead of the human. Threehalves is still a developing robotics project, but it represents a strange glimpse into a future where dangerous jobs could be performed remotely — with a human controlling the machine from a distance. And honestly… it might be one of the creepiest robots ever built. 👁️ #threehalves #robot #baal #satyress #horrortok

Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

Un robot ganó los 400 metros en Beijing en 38.15 segundos, más rápido que cualquier humano en la historia.  Pero el dato inquietante no es la velocidad: es que nadie programó la forma en que corrió.  El sistema descubrió, por sí solo, un movimiento de brazos que ningún ingeniero diseñó, y esa capacidad de autoajustarse sin supervisión es, a la vez, la mayor promesa y el mayor riesgo de la próxima década de robótica. El video del robot Tien Kung Ultra se volvió viral por su zancada exagerada, un balanceo de brazos que muchos compararon con una animación japonesa.  Según sus desarrolladores, el gesto surgió durante el entrenamiento por refuerzo: el robot generó un efecto giroscópico con los brazos para contrarrestar la rotación de las caderas y mantener el equilibrio a máxima velocidad, una solución de física básica que llegó a descubrir sin instrucción humana.  Hace apenas un año, en la primera edición de estos juegos, el ganador de la misma prueba tardó un minuto con 28 segundos.  Hoy el tiempo es casi cincuenta segundos más rápido, una curva de mejora que revela algo más importante que el marcador. Proyectada a diez años, esa capacidad de autoajuste abre dos futuros que conviven. El primero es el de máquinas capaces de resolver, sin diseño previo, tareas hoy imposibles de programar de forma tradicional: moverse en terrenos irregulares, operar en desastres, cubrir la escasez de mano de obra en logística y manufactura.  El segundo es más incómodo. Un sistema que reinventa su propio comportamiento en semanas es, por definición, más difícil de predecir y auditar. Cuanta más autonomía se les otorgue en fábricas, calles y hogares, más urgente será entender qué decisiones están tomando por cuenta propia y por qué.  A eso se suma una dimensión geopolítica: China respalda esta carrera con estrategia de Estado, y quien domine primero esta capacidad de autoajuste no solo tendrá robots más veloces, sino una ventaja industrial difícil de revertir. El video es gracioso. La curva de aprendizaje detrás es el verdadero titular.

China's LIFELIKE Robot Face Will Make You Question Everything #news #technology #china #robot  Chinese startup AheadForm has built a humanoid robot head that is nearly impossible to distinguish from a real human face. Powered by thirty precision brushless micro motors embedded beneath bionic silicone skin, the robot controls every blink, every glance, and every subtle micro expression with stunning accuracy. Cameras integrated directly into the eyes allow the robot to track faces in real time, while an onboard AI system reads human emotions and responds instantly with matching expressions. This is not a CGI render or a movie prop. This is real technology being developed right now in China for deployment in customer service, healthcare, and personal companionship. A viral video of the robot posted in March 2026 reignited a global conversation about whether hyper realistic robot faces are the missing key to making humanoid robots commercially successful. AheadForm believes the future of human robot interaction depends not just on what robots can do, but on how real they feel. The face of the future just got a lot harder to spot.

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.
